justification:
Technical round 1 for /oop-design/strategy-observer-decorator/. `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/oop-design/strategy-observer-decorator.md` from this worktree, run three times: PASS, blocks=23, executed=12, byte-identical result each run, no flakiness.

Every runnable sample was independently re-implemented from scratch with my own type/variable names (never copy-pasted from the article) and compiled/run on .NET 10.0.401: (1) the IComparer<T>-driven InsertionSort<T> (own Person/TeamOrder types) -- output matches; (2) the delegate-based Strategy (Func<IEnumerable<T>,string>) -- matches; (3) the Comparison<T> delegate overload of Sort -- matches; (4) the hand-built IObservable<T>/IObserver<T> SensorHub with using-scoped unsubscribe -- matches, including the fan-out/dispose timing (ThresholdAlert stops receiving after its using block, ConsoleDisplay keeps receiving); (5) the LimitedObserver<T> exercise solution -- matches; (6) BufferedStream's deferred-write behavior -- matches; (7) the GZipStream round-trip -- matches; (8) the hand-built CountingStream decorator wrapping GZipStream -- matches, byte counts equal on both directions; (9) the leaveOpen/disposal-cascade ObjectDisposedException exercise -- reproduced, throws exactly as claimed.

The pitfall box's specific empirical claim -- that Publish must snapshot _observers via .ToArray() before iterating, because mutating the live list mid-foreach (e.g. an observer disposing its own subscription inside OnNext) throws InvalidOperationException -- was independently tested both ways: with the snapshot it's silent and correct; removing it and constructing a self-unsubscribing observer reliably throws InvalidOperationException on my own from-scratch reproduction. This is a real, verified pitfall, not an assumed one.

All cited Microsoft Learn pages were fetched live (not trusted from the article) and checked quote-by-quote: List<T>.Sort's page states, verbatim, "This implementation performs an unstable sort; that is, if two elements are equal, their order might not be preserved" -- the article's quoted fragment "if two elements are equal, their order might not be preserved" is an exact substring, and the insertion-sort/heapsort/quicksort partition breakdown the article paraphrases matches the page's own bulleted description. The events page states, verbatim, "Events in .NET are based on the delegate model. The delegate model follows the observer design pattern" -- exact match (article drops only the markdown link syntax around the linked terms, which is standard when quoting linked prose). IObservable<T>'s Remarks state, verbatim, "The IObserver<T> and IObservable<T> interfaces provide a generalized mechanism for push-based notification, also known as the observer design pattern" -- the article's quoted fragment is an exact match. The observer-design-pattern page's BaggageHandler sample (fetched and read in full) does snapshot _observers into an array before iterating and calling OnNext on each entry, which is functionally the identical defensive pattern the article attributes to it -- HashSet<T>, like List<T>, throws InvalidOperationException on mutation during enumeration, so the snapshot protects against both concurrent-thread mutation (the sample's own stated motivation, via its Lock) and same-thread reentrant mutation (an observer unsubscribing itself from inside OnNext, the article's scenario); both are the same underlying enumeration-invalidation hazard, so "for the identical reason" holds up under scrutiny rather than being a stretch. BufferedStream's page states, verbatim, both "can be composed around certain types of streams" and "is designed to prevent the buffer from slowing down input and output when the buffer is not needed" -- both exact matches. GZipStream's page states, verbatim, "If the source data is already compressed, using these classes may actually increase the size of the stream" -- the article's quoted fragment is an exact match; its constructor pages state, verbatim, "By default, GZipStream owns the underlying stream, so closing the stream parameter also closes the underlying stream," which is exactly the leaveOpen-disposal-cascade behavior the article's callout and the ObjectDisposedException exercise both depend on and which I reproduced independently. Stream's "Notes to Implementers" section lists exactly the ten members the article claims a subclass must supply (CanRead, CanSeek, CanWrite, Flush, Length, Position, Seek, SetLength, Read, Write) and its "Derived" list confirms both System.IO.BufferedStream and System.IO.Compression.GZipStream inherit directly from Stream, matching the article's claim precisely.

GoF check, done specifically because the writer flagged it as a deliberate constraint: the article never places quotation marks around any Gamma/Helm/Johnson/Vlissides text. Both references to the book ("Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides catalogue this shape as Strategy, one of the behavioral patterns" and "...Decorator, one of the structural patterns") cite it only for pattern-name/chapter classification, and that classification is itself correct (Strategy is Behavioral, Decorator is Structural in the actual GoF taxonomy). No fabricated or misattributed quote exists anywhere in the article -- every quoted fragment traces to a live source that says exactly that.

Code idiom and correctness read cleanly throughout: InsertionSort<T>'s stability proof (moves an element only when the comparer returns strictly > 0, so tied elements are never swapped past each other) is the standard, correct argument for why that shift condition yields a stable sort, and is exercised directly in the 'Explain the tie' solution. The complexity claims (O(n log n) for List<T>.Sort's introspective sort, O(n^2) worst case for the hand-rolled insertion sort) are standard, uncontroversial algorithms facts; the O(n log n) figure specifically is not itself present in the cited MS Learn page (which lists the partition thresholds but not a Big-O figure), so it rests on general CS background rather than the citation -- accurate, but worth a one-line explicit note for a maximally rigorous reader (see issues).

Not a 10: this is thorough, verified, and differentiated (BCL-grounded pattern coverage most GoF-pattern tutorials don't attempt, plus a pitfall the writer verified by reproduction rather than assertion), but I found no comparably strong differentiation move to the interfaces-vs-abstract-classes round's live-documentation-error catch -- there was no MS documentation error to find here, and the article doesn't reach for one. That is not a fault, just the ceiling on this round: no factual error, fabricated quote, or non-running code was found anywhere in the article after an exhaustive independent pass.

issues.location: Strategy section, the paragraph beginning "`InsertionSort<T>` never mentions `Employee`, `Department`, or `Salary`"
issues.problem: The claim that `List<T>.Sort`'s introspective sort runs in O(n log n) time is standard, correct algorithms knowledge, but it is not itself present in the cited MS Learn page (source [2]), which lists the partition-size thresholds and named algorithms (insertion sort, heapsort, quicksort) without stating a Big-O figure. A rigorous reader who checks the citation for this specific number won't find it there.
issues.fixLooksLike: One clause making clear the O(n log n) figure is the well-known complexity of introspective sort generally rather than something MS Learn's page itself states, e.g. "...in O(n log n) time -- the standard bound for introspective sort, though the cited page states the partition strategy rather than a complexity figure directly."
